body: I grew up in Gaindakot, a small town on the Narayani River in Nepal, between my grandfather's tractor and my father's engine-parts shop. (The tractor is older than my father.)

I started college in physics at Truman State in Missouri, then moved to WashU through the 3+2 dual-degree engineering program to finish mechanical engineering. Now I study how coolant moves through battery cold plates, and I'm applying to PhD programs for Fall 2027.

Learning to know whether a simulation is right, not just whether it runs.

paradox.title: The best number my optimizer ever gave me was useless.
paradox.body: I let a topology optimizer redesign a whole serpentine cold plate with one goal: lose as little pressure as possible. It cut pressure loss by 87%. It did that by sending the coolant along the shortest route, so it reached only 16% of the plate.
paradox.after: I was glad, not surprised. The optimizer was finally behaving logically, and it proved that pressure alone is the wrong objective.
paradox.quote: An optimizer answers exactly the question you ask it, and nothing more.
paradox.figAlt: Two simulation results from Navin's poster. Top: with the original baffles kept, the optimizer only rounds the turns. Bottom: with the whole plate free, coolant takes a short path across one end and most of the plate sees almost no flow.
paradox.caption: From my SURGE poster. (a) Baffles kept: turns rounded, pressure loss −0.1%. (b) Whole plate free: pressure loss −87%, but the flow takes a shortcut.

teaching.body: Besides research, teaching is what I enjoy most. I'm an Undergraduate Teaching Fellow at WashU. I've supported Statics & Mechanics of Materials, Solid Mechanics and Thermodynamics (80–150 students per course), and I led J-Term sessions in Statics and Mechanics of Materials. Before that I tutored calculus and physics at Truman.
